stories.bridge: Hoffman bet that the résumé belongs on the network. This module is about making that bet pay for you — as a forward-deployed professional. Let's build the profile that gets found.

figures.name: Reid Hoffman
figures.role: Founder of LinkedIn; member of the 'PayPal mafia'

stories.hook: In December 2002, Reid Hoffman started a company on a contrarian bet: professionals would put their résumés on the internet.
stories.narrative: Hoffman had been an executive at PayPal — part of the 'PayPal mafia' that went on to found YouTube, Tesla, Palantir, SpaceX, and more — and he had watched social networks emerge for friendship and dating. Nobody was building one for work, partly because it seemed absurd: why would professionals publish their employment history where competitors, recruiters, and bosses could see it? Who would endorse a colleague in public? Hoffman founded LinkedIn in December 2002 and launched it on May 5, 2003, essentially from his living room, with a team that invited their own contacts one by one. Growth was slow at first — the classic cold-start problem — but the logic compounded relentlessly: every profile made the network more useful for recruiters, and every recruiter made having a profile more valuable for professionals. Endorsements, recommendations, the newsfeed, the recruiter seat: each feature tightened the loop. By the time Microsoft acquired LinkedIn in 2016 for $26.2 billion, it had become the professional graph of record — where hiring happens, where reputations are verified, where a forward-deployed engineer gets discovered by clients who never posted a job. The lesson for your career is Hoffman's original insight, and it's the thesis of this module: in a networked labor market, your work is only as visible as your profile makes it. Credentials matter, but discoverability compounds. The portfolio you build here — the projects, the writing, the proof of work — is your node in that graph. Make it dense, make it verifiable, and make it findable. The cold start was brutal: for months the site grew one invitation at a time, and the founders seeded it with their own networks. Hoffman's insight was that professionals would pay in data for access — to recruiters, to opportunities, to each other — and the exchange needed a trusted ledger. Your profile is that ledger entry. In this module you'll learn to make it the kind a hiring manager can't ignore.

stories.bridge: Stop planning, start experimenting — that is the entrepreneurial method. Now let's apply it to your own venture thinking.

figures.name: Steve Blank
figures.role: Entrepreneur and educator; originated customer development

stories.hook: In 2011, Eric Ries told founders to stop writing business plans and start running experiments.
stories.narrative: Ries had learned the expensive way. At IMVU, the startup he co-founded in 2004, the team spent months building an elaborate product based on assumptions — and launched to indifference. The classic failure mode: building something nobody wanted, efficiently. Rebuilding around a different method, he began codifying what actually worked: build the smallest thing that tests your riskiest assumption, measure real customer behavior, learn, and repeat — build, measure, learn. He drew on Steve Blank's 'customer development' methodology, forged in Silicon Valley's trenches: startups are not smaller versions of big companies but temporary organizations searching for a repeatable business model, and the founder's job is to get out of the building and test. In September 2011 Ries published 'The Lean Startup,' and the loop became the industry's operating system: the minimum viable product, the pivot (a change in strategy without a change in vision), the relentless preference for evidence over opinion. Enterprises adopted it, governments adopted it, nonprofits adopted it — the method escaped the startup entirely. The method's power for you is that it treats a career like a product: your portfolio projects are MVPs testing what the market values, interviews are customer discovery, and the market's response is data to learn from rather than verdicts to fear. This module teaches entrepreneurship as a discipline of validated learning — because the founders who survive are the ones who, like Ries at IMVU, learn to love being wrong quickly and cheaply. Blank's contribution is often under-credited: his "Four Steps to the Epiphany" (2005) argued that startups search while companies execute — a distinction Ries turned into the build-measure-learn loop. The method has since been formalized, taught, and occasionally cargo-culted; the cargo-cult version skips the hard part, which is the learning. Measure honestly, or the loop is theater. The loop only works if you respect every step — especially the learning.
stories.title: The story behind the Lean Startup
verifiedClaims: The method builds on Steve Blank's customer development

stories.bridge: Every negotiation, auction, and market you touch as a quant is a game in von Neumann's sense. Now let's learn the mathematics of strategic thinking.
stories.hook: In 1944, John von Neumann published the mathematics of bluffing.
stories.narrative: Von Neumann — the same mind behind the stored-program computer architecture and the mathematics of the atomic bomb — had been fascinated by poker for years: a game where optimal play requires randomness, deception, and precise calculation, where the best strategy is to be unpredictable on purpose. With the economist Oskar Morgenstern he wrote 'Theory of Games and Economic Behavior,' published in 1944: a formal mathematics of strategic interaction, where each player's best move depends on what the others do, and where the minimax theorem proves that even in pure conflict there is a rational way to play. It was abstract, formidable, and mostly ignored by economists — until the Cold War made it indispensable. RAND Corporation strategists used game theory to think about nuclear deterrence and escalation; Thomas Schelling used it to think about negotiation and credible threats. Then in 1950, a 21-year-old Princeton graduate student named John Nash defined the equilibrium that bears his name: the stable point where no player can profit by changing strategy alone — the generalization that made the theory apply to cooperation as well as conflict. Game theory went on to reshape economics (Nash's 1994 Nobel Prize), evolutionary biology (the logic of animal conflict), and — crucially for this module — finance: auctions, market-making, and algorithmic trading are games in von Neumann's exact sense, with payoffs, strategies, and equilibria. The quant ladder you're climbing is built on this mathematics. Von Neumann started from a card table; the industry ends at the order book. Learn to think in strategies, not just in prices. Von Neumann's minimax theorem — the proof that every finite game has a rational solution — was published in 1928, sixteen years before the book, and it came from thinking about parlor games. Schelling won his Nobel in 2005 for showing the same mathematics governs nuclear standoffs and neighborhood segregation. The quant's edge is seeing the game inside the market: everyone else sees prices; you see strategies.
stories.title: The story behind game theory
